title: The unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35)
hook: forgiven a fortune, he throttles a man who owes him pocket change
tomorrow: the Pharisee and the tax collector

segments.voice: Yesterday's fool wasn't stupid; he lived as if God weren't there, building bigger barns.

Peter thinks he's being generous. How many times do I have to forgive my brother? Seven times? Jesus says: not seven. "Until seventy times seven." Then he tells a story. A king is settling his accounts, and a servant is brought in who owes ten thousand talents. That's the talent from two days ago; ten thousand is a debt no servant could ever pay. The king orders him sold, with his wife and children. The servant falls on his knees and begs for time. The king, moved with compassion, doesn't give him time. He cancels the whole debt. In the street, the free man meets a fellow servant who owes him a hundred silver coins.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES? SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN.` → `TEN THOUSAND TALENTS.` → `THE WHOLE DEBT, CANCELED.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, he "took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." A hundred silver coins was real money; in the vineyard story, one coin was a day's wage. Next to what he'd just been let off, it's pocket change. And the other man falls down and begs with almost the same words: have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. That echo is the point. He hears his own prayer coming back at him, and doesn't recognize it. He has the man thrown in prison. The other servants, upset, go to the king. The king calls him back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" The ending is hard. The king hands him over to be punished until he pays, and Jesus says the Father will do the same to anyone who doesn't forgive from the heart. Christians don't soften that, but they often hear the warning as the flip side of the gift: mercy received is meant to keep moving. It's the shape of the Lord's Prayer: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. The Greek of Jesus's answer to Peter can be read as seventy times seven or seventy-seven, and translators still differ. Either way it means: stop counting. Some Christian teachers add that forgiving a debt doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen, or staying where you'll be hurt. It means letting go of the throat.
screen: `HE TOOK HIM BY THE THROAT.` · `THE SAME WORDS, COMING BACK.` · `AS I HAD PITY ON THEE.` · `SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN: STOP COUNTING.` · then, large: `MERCY IS MEANT TO KEEP MOVING.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone could have held something over you and didn't: a friend who never mentioned the money, a teacher who gave you another chance. Stay with how it felt to walk out free; if you pray, give thanks for them, and if you don't, rest in the gratitude. Then, gently, notice who owes you something small.
Talent. A fortune in silver, the coin so large that ten thousand of them was a debt no servant could ever hope to repay.
Your line: pass the mercy on. Mercy that stops with you isn't finished. Rest well tonight.

screen: `DAY 31 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PHARISEE AND THE TAX COLLECTOR.`

howItsDone: Christians ask God's forgiveness and pledge to forgive others every time they pray the Lord's Prayer ("forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors"), and churches often read this parable when teaching about forgiveness and reconciliation.

what a scholar hears: the Greek of Peter's answer can mean seventy-seven or seventy times seven, and Bibles still differ. either way it echoes Lamech's seventy-sevenfold revenge in Genesis 4, turned inside out.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: cut 'twenty years' wages' and 'like owing a billion dollars' from the hook; 'about a hundred days' work' now tied to the vineyard story's day's wage (Matthew 20:2); invented 'an hour earlier' cut; 'most hear' and 'many Christian teachers' softened; howItsDone 'many churches' softened.
A hundred pence (denarii) given as 'a hundred silver coins, about a hundred days' work'; ten thousand talents likened to 'a billion dollars' as a rough picture. Confirm the comparison is acceptable.

'Seventy times seven' vs 'seventy-seven': the Greek hebdomēkontakis hepta is read both ways; many modern translations prefer seventy-seven. Stated without ranking. Trapdoor links it to Lamech (Genesis 4:24), a common observation; confirm.
The hard ending (18:34–35, handed to the tormentors) is summarized plainly; confirm the framing 'the flip side of its gift'.

The line that forgiving 'doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen, or staying where you'll be hurt' is attributed to 'many Christian teachers'; added for listeners with abuse in their past. Confirm wording.
